habitat: Sumatran orangutans are found exclusively on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, primarily in the northern province of Aceh, inhabiting lowland tropical rainforests, peat swamps, and riverine forests at elevations below 1,000 meters. Their habitat is characterized by year-round high rainfall (2,000-4,000 mm annually), dense multi-layered canopies, and a rich diversity of fruiting trees. They are the most arboreal of the great apes, spending over 95% of their time in trees. Deforestation for palm oil, logging, and road construction has reduced their habitat by over 60% in the past 50 years.
diet: Sumatran orangutans are primarily frugivorous, with fruit making up 60-90% of their diet depending on season. Figs are a particularly important staple. They also consume leaves, bark, flowers, honey, insects, and occasionally bird eggs. During fruit-scarce periods, they rely on bark and leaves as fallback foods. They are important seed dispersers — the seeds of consumed fruit pass through their digestive system and are deposited throughout the forest in their feces, helping regenerate the rainforest ecosystem.
behavior: Sumatran orangutans are semi-solitary, with the strongest social bond being between mother and offspring — one of the longest mother-infant bonds in the animal kingdom, lasting 6-8 years. Males are largely solitary with large home ranges. Both sexes build a new sleeping nest each night from branches, leaves, and twigs. They demonstrate remarkable tool use in the wild: using sticks to extract honey and insects, leaves as gloves or umbrellas, and modifying twigs for specific tasks. They are cultural animals — different populations exhibit learned behaviors unique to their group, transmitted across generations.
facts: Sumatran orangutans are critically endangered, with fewer than 14,000 remaining. They have longer, more vibrant reddish-orange hair than Bornean orangutans and narrower faces with longer beards. Males develop distinctive cheek pads (flanges) at 15-20 years of age. The word 'orangutan' comes from Malay 'orang hutan' meaning 'person of the forest.' They share 97% of their DNA with humans. They give birth only once every 8-9 years — the longest interbirth interval of any land mammal.
naming: Sumatran orangutan names might reflect their red hair, arboreal lifestyle, or Indonesian heritage. Consider names like Sumatra, Aceh, Hutan (forest in Indonesian), Api (fire), Ember, Rusty, Canopy, Rafflesia (after the famous Sumatran flower), Merah (red in Indonesian), or Wana (forest in Javanese).
